There is fittle doubt that Congress cares about the distinction between 
“independent agencies” and the rest of the executive estabfishment. For 
example, the Paperwork Reduction Act, 44 U.S.C. §§ 3501 et seq., authorizes 
0MB to approve “information collection requests” by executive agencies. The 
Act then defines “information collection requests” to include any “written 
report form, apphcation form, schedule, questionnaire, reporting or 
recordkeeping requirement, collection of information requirement, or other 
similar method calling for the collection of information.” 44 U.S.C. § 3502(11). 
0MB may also review “information collection requests” by independent 
regulatory agencies, as enumerated in 44 U.S.C.§ 3502(5), but with a critical 
difference. Such agencies may, by majority vote, reject OMB’s disapprovals of 
their collection initiatives. 44 U.S.C. § 3507(f).

ConstitutioTbality of the HecLgoTi Orders. President Reagan’s issuance 
of Executive Order 12,291 provoked scholarly debate about the 
constitutionality of his initiative under Youngstown. Compare Morton 
Rosenberg, Presidential Control of Agency Rulemaking: An Analysis of 
Constitutional Issues That May Be Raised By Executive Order 12,291, 23 Ar iz . 
L. Re v . 1199 (1981) and Morton Rosenberg, Beyond the Limits of Executive 
Power: Presidential Control of Agency Rulemaking Under Executive Order 
12,291, 80 Mic h . L. Re v . 193 (1981) (challenging the constitutionality of the 
Order), with Peter M. Shane, Presidential Regulatory Oversight and the 
Separation of Powers: The Legality of Executive Order No. 12,291, 23 Ar iz . L. 
Re v . 1235 (1981) (supporting the Order).
The program is now over four decades old and has been implicated in a 
host of judicial review proceedings that have failed to cast doubt on its 
constitutionality. Moreover, since the promulgation of Executive Order No. 
12,291, Congress has enacted several statutes that either demand cost-benefit 
analyses of certain categories of rules, or that provide, in the case of the 
Congressional Review of Agency Rulemaldng Act, 5 U.S.C. § 801, that any cost-
benefit analyses prepared with regard to a rule be made available to Congress. 
Such provisions, especially the latter, might be thought to provide whatever 
congressional ratification that Ybun^s^orz^n-muided Justices might need in 
order to uphold the initiatives of the Carter through Obama Administrations 
with regard to presidential regulatory oversight.
